cards.text: The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, has watched righteous men get what the wicked deserve, and he admits no one can figure out the work done under the sun (Ecclesiastes 1:1; 8:14, 17). So he takes ALL of it to heart. And he lands somewhere.

cards.question: After taking all this to heart, where does the Teacher say the righteous and the wise, and their deeds, are?
The Teacher says people know what lies ahead of them, whether love or hate.

cards.text: Then he lines people up in pairs: the righteous and the wicked, the clean and the unclean, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. Total opposites, like a fresh batch and the batch I forgot was in the oven.

cards.question: The Teacher lines up opposites like the righteous and the wicked, and the good and the bad. What does he say about them?

answers.text: They all answer to the king

cards.text: He doesn't soften it one bit: there is one fate for everyone. Then he takes a hard look at people while they're still alive.

cards.question: The Teacher says that while men are alive, their hearts are full of evil and madness.

cards.text: And afterward, the Teacher says, they join the dead. He calls that one fate for everyone an evil in everything that is done under the sun.
But hold on, because he says there is hope for anyone who is among the living. And he backs it up with two animals.

cards.question: The Teacher says a live dog is better than a dead lion.
The Teacher explains what the living have going for them. What does he say the living know?

cards.text: The living know they will die. But the Teacher says the dead know nothing.

cards.question: Why does the Teacher say the dead have no further reward?

answers.text: The memory of them is forgotten

cards.question: The Teacher says the love, the hate and the envy of the dead have already vanished.

cards.text: And he says they will never again have a share in all that is done under the sun. Heavy stuff, friend, but stay with me, because the Teacher isn't done talking.
After all that talk about the dead, the Teacher turns to the living. And he starts with bread and wine.

cards.question: The Teacher says to go eat your bread with ___ and drink your wine with a cheerful heart.
The Teacher says to eat your bread with joy because God has already approved your works.

cards.text: Then he says, "Let your garments always be white, and never spare the oil for your head." Always white? Friend, between this apron and all the flour on me, I've got THAT part handled.

cards.question: The Teacher keeps going with how to live under the sun. Who does he say to enjoy life with?
The Teacher calls the life God has given you under the sun long and lasting.

cards.text: The Teacher calls them "all your fleeting days." And he says, "For this is your portion in life and in your labor under the sun."
Then he turns to whatever you find to do with your hands. Mixing, stamping, packing cookie boxes, you name it.

cards.question: How does the Teacher say to do whatever you find to do with your hands?
Why does the Teacher say to do your work with all your might?

answers.text: In Sheol there is no work

cards.text: In Sheol, he says, there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom. Then the Teacher says he saw something else under the sun, and it's about who comes out on top.

cards.question: The Teacher says the race goes to the swift and the battle goes to the strong.

cards.text: Same goes for bread, wealth and favor: they don't go to the wise, the intelligent and the skillful. It's like leaving for work early and STILL losing to the guy who left late and hit every green light.

cards.question: The Teacher says the race isn't to the swift or the battle to the strong, because time and ___ happen to all.

cards.text: And surely no man knows his time. Then the Teacher paints one more picture of how an evil time can fall on people.

cards.question: What does the Teacher say men ensnared in an evil time are like?

answers.text: Fish caught in a cruel net

cards.text: Like fish caught in a net or birds trapped in a snare, the Teacher says, men are ensnared in an evil time that suddenly falls upon them.
